content.es:
A “Black Hole Star” Could Reveal How the First Supermassive Black Holes Were Born

Astronomers have identified an extraordinary cosmic object, known as MoM-BH-1, that may represent a previously unrecognized type of astrophysical system.* Observed with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the object existed only about 660 million years after the Big Bang and displays a combination of features that cannot be easily explained by a conventional star or galaxy.

“The spectrum of this object is unlike anything we have seen before.”

An Object at Cosmic Dawn

MoM-BH*-1 is located at a redshift of approximately z = 7.76, meaning that the light reaching JWST today was emitted when the universe was still extremely young.

The object appears remarkably compact. Its observed properties indicate the presence of a supermassive black hole surrounded by an extraordinarily dense envelope of gas.

Rather than seeing the black hole directly, astronomers are observing the radiation produced by material surrounding it.

The basic picture is:

Dense gas → Accretion → Black hole → Energy release → Radiation

As matter falls toward a black hole, gravitational energy is converted into radiation. The process can be described approximately by:

L ≈ ηṀc²

where:

  • L = luminosity;
  • η = radiative efficiency;
  • Ṁ = mass-accretion rate;
  • c = the speed of light.

Because the speed of light is enormous, the c² term makes accretion an extraordinarily powerful source of energy.


A Strange Combination of Stellar and Black-Hole Features

What makes MoM-BH*-1 particularly unusual is its spectrum.

The object exhibits extremely broad hydrogen emission lines, including Hβ, which are characteristic of rapidly moving gas around an active black hole.

At the same time, it displays an exceptionally strong Balmer break, a spectral feature traditionally associated with stellar populations.

The measured Balmer break is approximately:

7.7×

For comparison, ordinary stellar populations generally cannot produce such an extreme feature. The researchers therefore argue that the observed spectrum is very difficult to explain through stars alone.

The Key Spectral Features


FeatureConventional starsActive black holesMoM-BH*-1
Balmer breakPossibleUnusualExtreme
Broad Hβ emissionRareCommonPresent
Dense surrounding gasVariableCommonExtreme
Point-like morphologyPossibleCommonYes
Strong variabilityPossibleCommonTentative evidence
Early-universe originPossiblePossiblez ≈ 7.76


The simultaneous presence of these characteristics is what makes the object so difficult to classify.


The “Black Hole Star” Hypothesis

To explain the observations, the researchers modeled MoM-BH*-1 as a black hole embedded within an extremely dense, turbulent envelope of gas.

The proposed structure is radically different from an ordinary star.

A conventional star is powered by nuclear fusion in its interior. A black hole star, by contrast, would obtain its energy from accretion onto the central black hole.

The surrounding gas would then absorb and reprocess that energy, producing an outer appearance that resembles a stellar atmosphere.

In simplified form:

Black hole → Accretion disk → Dense gas envelope → Reprocessed radiation

The model places the gaseous envelope on a scale of approximately 10–100 AU.

For comparison:

1 AU ≈ 149.6 million km

so an envelope extending tens of astronomical units would be comparable to the scale of our own Solar System.

A Different Kind of “Star”

It is important to clarify that a black hole star is not a conventional star containing a black hole.

Instead, the term describes a proposed configuration in which:

  1. A massive black hole provides the central energy source.
  2. Matter rapidly falls toward the black hole.
  3. Extremely dense gas surrounds the central engine.
  4. The gas absorbs and re-emits the radiation.
  5. The resulting spectrum contains both black-hole-like and star-like features.

This makes the object something of a physical hybrid:

Black-hole engine + stellar-like envelope = “black hole star”


The Mysterious Little Red Dots

The discovery may also help explain one of JWST's most intriguing discoveries: the population of compact objects known as little red dots (LRDs).

These objects are small, extremely red, and surprisingly abundant in observations of the early universe.

Their physical nature remains uncertain.

One possibility: some little red dots may be black holes embedded in dense gaseous environments.

MoM-BH*-1 is particularly useful because the radiation from the proposed black-hole component appears to dominate almost all of the observed light. This gives astronomers a relatively clean view of the central source.

The researchers suggest that similar objects embedded within brighter host galaxies could appear very different when observed from Earth.

In other words:

Black hole star + bright host galaxy → Little Red Dot

This possibility could help reconcile several otherwise puzzling properties of the LRD population.


Observation ≠ Interpretation

The discovery should nevertheless be interpreted carefully.

Astronomers have observed the object's spectrum, luminosity, morphology, and other properties.

The black hole star is the physical interpretation that currently provides a compelling explanation for those observations.

These are not the same thing.

A simplified scientific workflow is:

Observation → Hypothesis → Model → Prediction → New Observation → Confirmation or Refutation

The researchers therefore do not claim that JWST has directly photographed the interior of MoM-BH*-1.

Instead, they constructed detailed spectral models and found that an extremely dense gaseous envelope surrounding an accreting black hole can reproduce several of the object's unusual characteristics.


Why Did the Object Become Red?

The object's extreme redness is another important clue.

MoM-BH*-1 is surrounded by dense hydrogen gas. Radiation originating near the black hole interacts with this material before escaping into space.

The resulting spectrum contains a dramatic Balmer break, in which the observed flux changes sharply across a characteristic wavelength.

Hydrogen's atomic structure is responsible for the underlying physics.

The Balmer series involves transitions to the n = 2 energy level.

For example:

Hα: n = 3 → n = 2

Hβ: n = 4 → n = 2

Hγ: n = 5 → n = 2

These transitions provide astronomers with valuable information about the physical conditions of the gas.

In MoM-BH*-1, the absorption is extraordinarily strong, implying gas densities of approximately:

n<sub>H</sub> ≳ 10⁹ cm⁻³

That is an extreme physical environment.


A Possible Solution to an Old Cosmic Problem

One of the major problems in modern cosmology is explaining how supermassive black holes became so massive so quickly.

Today's largest black holes can reach masses of approximately:

M<sub>BH</sub> ≈ 10⁶–10⁹ M<sub>☉</sub>

where M<sub>☉</sub> represents the mass of the Sun.

For example:

  • 10⁶ M<sub>☉</sub> = one million solar masses
  • 10⁹ M<sub>☉</sub> = one billion solar masses

The problem becomes particularly severe when astronomers observe enormous black holes at very high redshifts.

There simply may not have been enough time for ordinary stellar-mass black holes to grow to such enormous sizes through conventional accretion alone.

The proposed black-hole-star phase could provide a possible solution.

Super-Eddington Growth

The researchers suggest that an early black hole embedded in extremely dense gas could undergo super-Eddington accretion.

The Eddington limit describes the approximate balance between gravitational attraction and radiation pressure.

In simplified terms:

Accretion rate > Eddington rate → rapid black-hole growth

If such conditions existed in the early universe, black holes could potentially gain mass much more rapidly than under standard growth scenarios.


What Could Happen Next?

If the black-hole-star interpretation is correct, MoM-BH*-1 may represent an early stage in the evolution of a much more familiar object.

One possible sequence is:

Black hole star → Growing supermassive black hole → Quasar → Massive galaxy

The object could therefore represent a transitional phase between the earliest black-hole seeds and the powerful quasars observed later in cosmic history.

The researchers also note that MoM-BH*-1 lies near another galaxy and that the two systems may eventually merge.

According to the models, such a merger could occur on a timescale of approximately 100 million years.


A New Window into the Early Universe

The significance of MoM-BH*-1 goes beyond the discovery of a strange object.

It demonstrates the extraordinary power of spectroscopy.

A single point of light can reveal:

  • the object's redshift;
  • the velocity of its gas;
  • the density of its surrounding material;
  • the presence of specific chemical elements;
  • the mechanisms producing its radiation;
  • and potentially the history of its central black hole.

The object may look like nothing more than a tiny red dot in an astronomical image.

But hidden inside that dot is a physical system that may have existed when the universe was less than 5% of its current age.

The universe may have been much stranger, and much more dynamic, than our simplest models suggest.


The Remaining Questions

Several important questions remain unanswered.

Is MoM-BH-1 genuinely the first confirmed black hole star?*

How common are these objects?

Could they explain a substantial fraction of the little red dots discovered by JWST?

How massive is the central black hole really?

How long can a black hole remain in this heavily enshrouded phase?

And perhaps most importantly:

Did black hole stars provide the seeds from which the universe's earliest supermassive black holes grew?

Future observations with JWST and other observatories will be crucial for testing these possibilities.

In Summary

MoM-BH-1 is one of the most unusual objects yet identified in the early universe.*

Its spectrum combines characteristics normally associated with stars and active black holes, while its extreme Balmer break and dense gaseous environment challenge conventional explanations.

The leading model describes a rapidly accreting black hole hidden inside an enormous envelope of dense, turbulent gas.

If confirmed, black hole stars could provide an important missing link in the story of how the first supermassive black holes formed.

For now, however, the most important conclusion is simpler:

JWST has found another object that forces astronomers to rethink what the early universe looked like.


Primary Reference

Kokorev et al. (2026), A gas-enshrouded and gas-reddened black hole at cosmic dawn, Nature, 656, 329–333.

title.es: Una “estrella de agujero negro” podría revelar cómo nacieron los primeros agujeros negros supermasivos
title.en: A “Black Hole Star” Could Reveal How the First Supermassive Black Holes Were Born

content.es:
Astrónomos han identificado un objeto cósmico extremadamente peculiar, denominado MoM-BH-1, que podría representar una nueva clase de objeto astrofísico. El descubrimiento, realizado mediante el Telescopio Espacial James Webb (JWST), podría ayudar a explicar cómo surgieron los primeros agujeros negros supermasivos.

“Este objeto nos ofrece una ventana hacia una etapa extremadamente temprana de la formación de agujeros negros.”

Un objeto en los albores del universo

MoM-BH*-1 se observa tal como era aproximadamente 660 millones de años después del Big Bang. Debido a que la luz necesita tiempo para viajar, observar este objeto equivale a mirar directamente hacia una etapa extremadamente temprana de la historia cósmica.

El objeto presenta una luminosidad extraordinaria. Los investigadores plantean que podría estar formado por un agujero negro supermasivo rodeado por una enorme envoltura de gas.

En este escenario, el agujero negro estaría absorbiendo materia mediante un proceso de acreción. La energía liberada calentaría el material circundante y produciría la intensa radiación que finalmente llega hasta nuestros telescopios.

¿Por qué es importante?

El descubrimiento plantea una pregunta fundamental:

¿Cómo pudieron existir agujeros negros con masas de millones o incluso miles de millones de veces la masa del Sol cuando el universo todavía era extremadamente joven?

Los modelos tradicionales proponen que los agujeros negros pueden comenzar a partir del colapso de estrellas masivas y crecer posteriormente mediante la acumulación de materia y fusiones.

Sin embargo, existe un problema: el tiempo disponible podría no ser suficiente para que un agujero negro formado de esta manera alcance las enormes masas observadas en el universo temprano.

La hipótesis de la “estrella de agujero negro”

Los investigadores proponen una estructura que combina propiedades asociadas con un agujero negro y una enorme envoltura gaseosa.

El proceso puede representarse de manera simplificada como:

Gas → Acreción → Agujero negro → Liberación de energía → Envoltura luminosa

La luminosidad producida por la acreción puede expresarse mediante:

L ≈ ηṀc²

donde:

  • L = luminosidad;
  • η = eficiencia de conversión de masa en energía;
  • Ṁ = tasa de acreción;
  • c = velocidad de la luz.

El término c² resulta particularmente importante. Debido a la enorme magnitud de la velocidad de la luz, incluso una cantidad relativamente pequeña de masa puede corresponder a una cantidad extraordinaria de energía.

Por ejemplo, la famosa relación de Einstein,

E = mc²,

establece la equivalencia entre masa y energía.

Comparación de propiedades

CaracterísticaEstrella convencionalAgujero negroMoM-BH*-1Fuente principal de energíaFusión nuclearAcreciónAcreciónSuperficie estelarSíNoNo convencionalGas circundanteVariableVariableMuy densoEmisión intensaSíSíSíPresencia en el universo tempranoSíSíSí

Los misteriosos little red dots

Desde las primeras observaciones del JWST, los astrónomos han identificado numerosos objetos compactos y rojizos conocidos como little red dots (LRDs).

Su naturaleza continúa siendo objeto de debate.

Hipótesis: algunos little red dots podrían corresponder a agujeros negros en crecimiento rodeados por enormes cantidades de gas.

Si esta interpretación resulta correcta, estos objetos podrían representar una fase temprana de la evolución de los agujeros negros supermasivos.

Los investigadores deberán determinar si esta población constituye una categoría física real o si los objetos observados corresponden a fenómenos diferentes que producen señales similares.

Observación ≠ interpretación

Es importante distinguir entre lo que los astrónomos han observado y la explicación propuesta para esas observaciones.

Los investigadores han detectado radiación y características espectroscópicas compatibles con el modelo propuesto. Sin embargo, afirmar que MoM-BH*-1 es definitivamente una “estrella de agujero negro” sería prematuro.

En ciencia, una observación puede ser sólida mientras que su interpretación permanece abierta.

Observación → Modelo → Predicción → Nueva observación → Confirmación o refutación

Este proceso constituye una de las bases del método científico.

¿Qué podría significar para la cosmología?

Si futuras observaciones confirman la existencia de estos objetos, podrían modificar nuestra comprensión de la formación de los primeros agujeros negros.

Una posible secuencia evolutiva sería:

Estrella de agujero negro → Agujero negro supermasivo → Cuásar → Evolución galáctica

Los agujeros negros supermasivos observados actualmente pueden alcanzar masas extraordinarias, del orden de:

M<sub>BH</sub> ≈ 10⁶–10⁹ M<sub>☉</sub>

donde M<sub>☉</sub> representa la masa solar.

Para poner estas magnitudes en perspectiva:

  • 10⁶ M<sub>☉</sub> = 1.000.000 masas solares
  • 10⁹ M<sub>☉</sub> = 1.000.000.000 masas solares

La diferencia entre ambas escalas es de un factor de 1.000.

Una cuestión todavía abierta

El descubrimiento de MoM-BH*-1 no resuelve por sí solo el problema del origen de los agujeros negros supermasivos.

Sin embargo, proporciona una nueva pieza de evidencia para estudiar una época del universo que, hasta hace relativamente poco tiempo, era prácticamente inaccesible.

El James Webb está permitiendo observar objetos cuya luz fue emitida cuando el universo tenía apenas una fracción de su edad actual.

“Cada nueva observación del universo temprano puede obligarnos a revisar modelos que parecían suficientemente sólidos.”

En síntesis

El James Webb no solamente está encontrando galaxias antiguas. También está revelando objetos cuya naturaleza puede obligarnos a reconsiderar cómo evolucionó el universo temprano.

La gran pregunta ahora es si MoM-BH*-1 constituye una rareza cósmica o el primer ejemplo de una población mucho más amplia.

La respuesta podría cambiar nuestra comprensión de cómo nacieron los primeros agujeros negros supermasivos.

Referencia principal

Kokorev et al. (2026), A gas-enshrouded and gas-reddened black hole at cosmic dawn, Nature.
